topics.h: In 2006, scientists voted that Pluto is no longer a full planet. Did Pluto change, or did our knowledge change?
p: Science is a way of finding out how the world works by observing, asking questions and testing ideas.
Scientific ideas are based on evidence. When strong new evidence appears, scientists improve or replace old ideas.
New tools like the telescope and the microscope let people see things they could never see before, so science grows.
Long ago many people believed the Earth was the centre of everything. Careful observations later showed that the Earth and other planets go around the Sun.
Science is never 'finished'. Every answer leads to new questions.

ex.q: A student says, 'If scientists keep changing their ideas, science must be unreliable.' Is that right?
st: Ask: why do scientists change an idea? Because new evidence is found.
Changing an idea to fit better evidence makes our knowledge more accurate, not less.
So the habit of checking and correcting is the strength of science.
ex.a: No. Science changes because it follows evidence, and that makes it more reliable over time.

topics.rl: Weather forecasts on TV keep getting better because scientists keep improving their models with new satellite data.

rv.summary: Science is a way of finding out how the world works by observing, asking and testing. Its ideas follow evidence, so they are improved when new evidence or new tools appear.

topics.h: India celebrates National Science Day every year on 28 February. Can you guess which discovery it remembers?
p: People from every part of the world, including India, have added to science.
C.V. Raman discovered how light scatters in a special way (the Raman effect) on 28 February 1928 and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.
Jagadish Chandra Bose built a very sensitive instrument, the crescograph, to measure the tiny growth of plants.
Scientists build on each other's work. One discovery often makes the next one possible.
Today science is often done by big teams, like the ISRO team whose Chandrayaan-3 lander touched down near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.

ex.q: Why did Chandrayaan-3 need people who knew maths, chemistry, physics, computers and more?
st: A Moon mission needs rockets (physics), fuel (chemistry), path calculations (maths) and control programs (computers).
No single person knows all of this well enough.
So people with different skills work as one team, using knowledge built by many people before them.
ex.a: Because big science problems need many kinds of knowledge working together.

topics.rl: The mobile phone in your home uses ideas from physics, chemistry, maths and engineering, discovered by people from many countries over hundreds of years.

rv.summary: People everywhere, including India, have added to science. Scientists build on each other's work, and today big projects like Chandrayaan-3 need teams from many subjects.

topics.h: Why does a steel tumbler of cold water 'sweat' on a hot day? Every great discovery starts with a 'why' like this!
p: Curiosity means wanting to know. Inquiry means finding out step by step.
The steps: observe, ask a question, make a guess you can test (a hypothesis), test it with an experiment, record results, draw a conclusion.
In a fair test you change only one thing (the variable you are testing) and keep everything else the same.
Record what really happens, even if it is different from what you expected.
Repeat the test to be sure your result is not just luck.

ex.q: Meena wants to test whether salt helps ice melt faster. She puts salt on one ice cube in the sun and no salt on another ice cube in the shade. Is this a fair test?
st: List what is different: salt and also sun versus shade.
Two things are changed, so we cannot tell which one made the ice melt faster.
Make it fair: keep both cubes the same size and in the same place; change only the salt.
ex.a: Not fair. She should change only one thing, the salt, and keep everything else the same.

topics.rl: Your doctor uses inquiry too: noticing symptoms, guessing the cause, ordering a test and then deciding the treatment.

topics.ch: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral
topics.h: Nimbu pani, imli chutney and dahi all taste sour. Is there a hidden science reason?
p: Acids usually taste sour. The word 'acid' comes from the Latin word 'acere', meaning sour.
Bases usually taste bitter and feel soapy or slippery when touched.
Substances that are neither acidic nor basic are called neutral, like sugar solution, common salt solution and pure water.
Food acids: lemon and orange have citric acid, curd has lactic acid, vinegar has acetic acid, tamarind has tartaric acid and amla has ascorbic acid (vitamin C).
Safety first: never taste or touch unknown substances in a lab. Some acids and bases are strong enough to burn skin.

ex.q: Soap solution feels slippery between the fingers and tastes bitter (please don't try!). Is it acidic, basic or neutral?
st: Acids are sour; bases are bitter and soapy to touch.
Soap solution feels soapy and is bitter.
So it matches the properties of a base.
ex.a: Soap solution is basic.

topics.rl: The sour taste of raw mango and the fizz in lemon with baking soda both come from acids at work in your kitchen.

rv.summary: Acids usually taste sour, bases taste bitter and feel soapy, and neutral substances are neither. Many foods contain acids, like citric acid in lemon and lactic acid in curd.

topics.ch: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral
topics.h: A yellow haldi stain on your school shirt turns red when you scrub it with soap. Magic? No, chemistry!
p: An indicator is a substance that shows by changing colour whether something is acidic, basic or neutral.
Litmus comes from lichens. Acids turn blue litmus red. Bases turn red litmus blue. Neutral solutions change neither.
Turmeric (haldi) is yellow. It turns red in a base and stays yellow in an acid or a neutral solution.
China rose (gudhal or hibiscus) petal extract turns dark pink (magenta) in an acid and green in a base.
Indicators are safer than tasting, so they are the scientist's tool for testing.

ex.q: A clear liquid turns red litmus blue. It does not change blue litmus. What is it, and what will turmeric paper do in it?
st: Red litmus turning blue means the liquid is a base.
Bases do not change blue litmus, which matches.
Turmeric turns red in a base.
ex.a: It is a base, and turmeric paper will turn red.

topics.rl: When you wash a turmeric (haldi) curry stain with soap, it turns red because soap is basic. After rinsing well with plenty of water, it turns yellow again.

rv.summary: Indicators change colour to show whether a substance is acidic, basic or neutral. Litmus, turmeric and china rose are natural indicators.

topics.ch: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral
topics.h: An ant bite stings because the ant injects an acid. What could cancel the sting?
p: When an acid and a base react, they cancel each other's effect. This is called neutralisation.
Acid + base gives salt + water, and heat is given out.
In neutralisation, 'salt' means a new substance formed from the acid and the base. Common salt is only one example.
Antacids such as milk of magnesia (a base) are used to relieve acidity in the stomach.
Ant bites contain formic acid. Rubbing moist baking soda or calamine solution (both mildly basic) on them helps.

ex.q: A farmer finds that the soil in his field is too acidic for his crops. What should he add, and why?
st: Acidic soil needs a base to neutralise it.
Quicklime (calcium oxide) or slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) are bases.
Adding them neutralises the extra acid, so the crops can grow better.
ex.a: He should add quicklime or slaked lime, which are bases that neutralise the acid in the soil.

topics.rl: If soil is too basic, farmers add organic matter like compost, which releases acids. Factories must neutralise acidic waste water with bases before letting it out.

rv.summary: Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base, giving a salt and water and releasing heat. It is used for acidity, ant bites, soil treatment and factory waste.

topics.h: A tiny torch cell has no wires to the wall, yet it can light a bulb. Where does its electricity come from?
p: An electric cell makes electricity from chemicals stored inside it. When the chemicals are used up, the cell stops working.
Every cell has two terminals: a positive (+) terminal, the metal cap, and a negative (−) terminal, the flat metal disc.
A torch bulb has a thin coiled wire called the filament. It glows when electricity flows through it. If the filament breaks, the bulb is 'fused'.
An LED (light emitting diode) has two wires. The longer one goes to the positive side. An LED glows only when connected the right way round.
A switch is a simple device that joins (ON) or breaks (OFF) the path of electricity.

ex.q: Raju connects a bulb to a new cell correctly, but it does not glow. Another bulb glows in the same set-up. What is wrong with the first bulb?
st: The cell is new and works, because another bulb glows.
So the problem is in the first bulb.
Look at its filament: if it is broken, electricity cannot pass through.
ex.a: The first bulb is fused: its filament is broken.

topics.rl: Torches, TV remotes, wall clocks and toys run on cells. Joining two or more cells together makes a battery, like the one in a mobile phone.

rv.summary: An electric cell makes electricity from stored chemicals and has a positive and a negative terminal. A bulb's filament glows when current flows, an LED glows only the right way round, and a switch joins or breaks the path.

topics.h: Electricity is like a racing track: it only flows if the track is a complete loop with no gaps!
p: A circuit is a complete, closed path for electricity: from the positive terminal of the cell, through wires and a bulb, back to the negative terminal.
If there is any gap, the circuit is open (or broken) and the bulb does not glow.
A switch in the ON position closes the circuit. In the OFF position it opens it.
Scientists draw circuits using symbols. In a cell symbol, the longer thin line is the positive terminal and the shorter thick line is the negative terminal.
A circuit diagram is quick to draw and easy for anyone in the world to read.

ex.q: A bulb is joined to a cell with two wires, but both wires touch only the positive terminal. Will the bulb glow?
st: For the bulb to glow, electricity must flow through a complete loop.
The loop must go from the positive terminal, through the bulb, to the negative terminal.
Here the negative terminal is not connected, so the path is not complete.
ex.a: No. The circuit is open, because the negative terminal is not connected.

topics.rl: When you press the switch of a fan at home, you complete a circuit. Electricians read circuit diagrams to wire buildings safely.

topics.h: Why does the screwdriver of an electrician have a plastic or rubber handle? Let's find out!
p: Materials that let electricity pass through them easily are called conductors. Metals like copper, aluminium and iron are good conductors.
Materials that do not let electricity pass easily are called insulators, like rubber, plastic, dry wood, glass and dry paper.
Graphite (the 'lead' of a pencil) is not a metal, but it conducts electricity.
Wires have a copper or aluminium core covered with a plastic coat. The metal carries the current; the plastic keeps us safe.
Our body can conduct electricity, so never touch switches with wet hands or play near electric poles. The mains supply in Indian homes is about 230 volts, which is dangerous.

ex.q: You make a tester: a cell, a bulb and two wires with a gap. You touch both free ends to a steel spoon and the bulb glows. Then you try a plastic ruler and it does not. What do you conclude?
st: The bulb glows only if the object completes the circuit.
The steel spoon completed it: it lets current pass.
The plastic ruler did not: it blocks current.
ex.a: Steel (a metal) is a conductor; plastic is an insulator.

topics.rl: Electricians wear rubber gloves and rubber-soled shoes, and switch boards are made of plastic, because these are insulators.

rv.summary: Conductors like metals let electricity pass easily; insulators like rubber, plastic, dry wood and glass do not. Graphite is a non-metal conductor. Our body conducts too, so we must stay safe.

topics.ch: The World of Metals and Non-metals
topics.h: The silver vark on a kaju katli is a metal sheet beaten so thin that you can eat it! How can a metal become that thin?
p: Lustre: metals have a shiny surface, especially when freshly cut or polished.
Malleable: metals can be beaten into thin sheets, like aluminium foil and silver vark.
Ductile: metals can be drawn into thin wires, like copper wires.
Sonorous: metals make a ringing sound when struck, which is why bells are made of metal.
Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Most are hard, but sodium and potassium are so soft they can be cut with a knife, and mercury is a liquid at room temperature.

ex.q: A shopkeeper hammers a lump of material and it spreads into a thin sheet without breaking. Then he taps it and it rings. Is it more likely a metal or a non-metal?
st: Spreading into a sheet when hammered is called malleability.
Ringing when struck is called sonority.
Both are typical properties of metals.
ex.a: It is most likely a metal.

topics.rl: A steel tiffin, copper wires in your house, a brass temple bell and aluminium foil around rotis all use special properties of metals.

rv.summary: Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile and sonorous, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. Most are hard solids, but sodium and potassium are soft and mercury is a liquid.

traps: Don't mix up malleable (sheets) and ductile (wires).
Not all metals are hard: sodium and potassium are soft.

topics.ch: The World of Metals and Non-metals
topics.h: Diamond, the hardest natural substance, and pencil 'lead' are both made of the same non-metal: carbon!
p: Non-metals are usually dull, not sonorous and poor conductors of heat and electricity.
Solid non-metals like sulphur and coal are brittle: they break or turn to powder when hammered.
Many non-metals are gases, such as oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen and chlorine. Bromine is a liquid non-metal.
Exceptions: iodine is a shiny non-metal, graphite conducts electricity, and diamond is very hard.
When metals burn in air they form oxides that are basic (they turn red litmus blue). Oxides of non-metals like sulphur are acidic (they turn blue litmus red).

ex.q: In a teacher's demonstration, a magnesium ribbon burns with a bright white light and leaves white ash. The ash is dissolved in water and tested with litmus. Which litmus changes, and why?
st: Magnesium is a metal, so its ash is magnesium oxide, a metal oxide.
Metal oxides make basic solutions.
Bases turn red litmus blue.
ex.a: Red litmus turns blue, because magnesium oxide forms a basic solution.

topics.rl: The oxygen we breathe, the nitrogen that fills chips packets and the chlorine used to clean drinking water are all non-metals.

rv.summary: Non-metals are usually dull, brittle when solid and poor conductors, and many are gases. Metal oxides are basic and non-metal oxides are acidic.

topics.ch: The World of Metals and Non-metals
topics.h: From the iron in railway tracks to the oxygen cylinders in hospitals, metals and non-metals keep India running!
p: Iron is used for buildings, bridges, railway tracks and machines (mostly as steel).
Copper and aluminium make electric wires; aluminium also makes foil, utensils and aeroplane parts because it is light.
Gold and silver are used in jewellery because they are lustrous and malleable, and gold keeps its shine for a very long time; silver is also beaten into vark for sweets.
Oxygen is needed for breathing; nitrogen is used to make fertilisers and to fill food packets; chlorine is used to clean drinking water.
Carbon (as graphite) is used in pencils, and iodine is used as an antiseptic on wounds.

ex.q: Why is the handle of a cooking pan made of wood or plastic, while the pan is made of metal?
st: The pan must pass heat to the food, so it needs a good conductor: a metal.
The handle must not get hot, so it needs a poor conductor.
Wood and plastic are poor conductors of heat.
ex.a: The metal pan conducts heat to the food; the wooden or plastic handle does not, so it stays safe to hold.

topics.rl: Look around your kitchen: steel utensils, an aluminium kadhai, a copper-bottom pot and plastic or wooden handles, all chosen for their properties.

topics.ch: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical
topics.h: You can melt ghee and set it again, but can you ever 'unfry' a puri? That is the difference between two kinds of change!
p: A physical change alters the shape, size or state of a substance, but no new substance is formed. Examples: melting ice, dissolving sugar, tearing paper.
Many physical changes can be reversed, but not all: torn paper stays torn, yet it is still paper.
A chemical change forms one or more new substances. Examples: burning, cooking, rusting, curdling of milk, ripening of fruit.
Signs of a chemical change: a gas is given off, the colour changes, heat or light is produced, or a new smell appears.
Some events have both: when a candle burns, the wax melts (physical) and also burns (chemical).

ex.q: Your teacher adds a spoon of baking soda to vinegar. It fizzes. When the gas is passed into lime water, the lime water turns milky. Is this a physical or a chemical change?
st: Fizzing shows a gas is being made.
The gas is carbon dioxide; it turns lime water milky by forming a new substance.
New substances are formed, so it is a chemical change.
ex.a: It is a chemical change: new substances such as carbon dioxide are formed.

topics.rl: Making dahi from milk, cooking dal, burning a diya and fruits ripening are chemical changes. Melting butter, making ice in the freezer and dissolving sugar in tea are physical changes.

topics.ch: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical
topics.h: The Iron Pillar in Delhi has stood for more than 1,600 years with very little rust. Yet a bicycle left in the rain gets rusty in weeks!
p: Rusting is a chemical change in which iron reacts with oxygen (from air) and water (or moisture) to form rust, a reddish-brown substance (iron oxide).
Both air and water are needed for rusting. Without either one, iron does not rust.
Rusting is faster in humid places and near the sea, where the air is moist and salty.
Rust is flaky. It falls off and exposes fresh iron, so the iron slowly gets eaten away.
We prevent rusting by painting, oiling or greasing, and by galvanisation (coating iron with zinc). Stainless steel, made by mixing iron with metals like chromium and nickel, does not rust easily.

ex.q: Three iron nails are kept: A in dry air (with a drying agent), B in boiled water covered with an oil layer, and C in a test tube with a little water and open to air. Which nail rusts?
st: A has air but no water.
B has water but the oil layer and boiling keep air out.
C has both air and water.
ex.a: Only nail C rusts, because rusting needs both air and water.

topics.rl: Iron gates and window grills are painted, bicycle chains are oiled, and buckets are galvanised so they last longer.

topics.ch: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical
topics.h: Mishri, the crystal sugar many families enjoy with saunf after meals, is made by a process called crystallisation!
p: Crystals are solids with regular shapes and flat, shiny faces. Salt, sugar, alum (phitkari) and copper sulphate form crystals.
Crystallisation is a way to get large, pure crystals of a substance from its solution.
Steps: dissolve as much of the substance as possible in hot water, filter it, then let it cool slowly without disturbing it.
Hot water can dissolve more of a substance than cold water, so crystals appear as the solution cools.
Crystallisation is a physical change: the substance stays the same, only its form changes.

ex.q: Salt can be got by drying sea water in the sun. Why do we need crystallisation to get pure salt?
st: When sea water evaporates, everything dissolved in it is left behind, not just salt.
So the salt has impurities mixed in.
In crystallisation, pure crystals form while impurities stay in the liquid or are filtered out.
ex.a: Evaporation leaves impurities behind with the salt; crystallisation gives pure crystals.

topics.rl: Sugar factories make clean sugar crystals, and mishri is made by slow crystallisation from thick sugar syrup.

topics.ch: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change
topics.h: Have you noticed that some classmates suddenly look taller after the summer holidays? Welcome to the growth spurt!
p: Adolescence is the stage of life between childhood and adulthood, the teenage years. The body and mind both change.
Puberty is the time when the body starts changing towards an adult body. It is controlled by hormones, chemical messengers made in the body.
Common changes: a sudden increase in height (growth spurt), new hair growth, more sweat and oil, and a changing voice.

In boys the voice box grows and the voice becomes deeper; it may crack for a while. A bump in the throat called the Adam's apple may show. In girls, the body shape changes and periods (menstruation) begin, which is a normal, healthy process.
Changes start at different ages for different people. Girls often begin a little earlier than boys. All of this is normal.

ex.q: Aman is shorter than most of his friends in Class 7 and feels worried. What would you tell him?
st: Puberty and the growth spurt start at different ages in different people.
Many children grow quickly a little later.
Height also depends on family genes, food, sleep and exercise.
ex.a: There is no need to worry: everyone has their own timing, and eating well, sleeping well and staying active help growth.

topics.rl: Doctors and school health check-ups track height and weight to make sure children are growing in a healthy way.

rv.summary: Adolescence is the stage between childhood and adulthood. During puberty, hormones bring changes like a growth spurt, new hair, more sweat and oil, a changing voice and, in girls, periods. Timing differs for everyone.

topics.ch: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change
topics.h: Your body is like a new phone getting a big update during adolescence. It needs the right care to run smoothly!
p: More sweat and oil means you should bathe daily, wear clean, washed clothes and keep your hair clean.
Wash your face gently to help with pimples. Do not squeeze them, as this can cause marks and infection.
Girls should use clean sanitary pads or clean cloth during periods, change them regularly, and wrap and throw them in a dustbin.
Eat a balanced diet: proteins for growth, calcium (milk, curd, ragi) for bones, and iron (green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses) for healthy blood.
Get enough sleep, play or exercise every day, and drink plenty of water. Avoid too much junk food and fizzy drinks.

ex.q: Kavya has started her periods and feels very tired. Her doctor says she needs more iron. Which tiffin is better: chips and a cold drink, or a roti with palak dal and a few dates?
st: Iron is needed to make healthy blood, and some blood is lost during periods.
Palak (spinach), dal and dates contain iron.
Chips and cold drinks give little iron or other nutrients.
ex.a: The roti with palak dal and dates is better, because it gives iron and other nutrients.

topics.rl: Under a government health programme, many schools in India give adolescents weekly iron and folic acid tablets, because iron is so important at this age.

rv.summary: Adolescents need extra care for hygiene: daily baths, clean clothes, gentle face washing and clean pads during periods. A balanced diet with protein, calcium and iron, plus sleep, exercise and water, keeps them healthy.

topics.ch: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change
topics.h: One moment you feel on top of the world, the next you are upset over a small thing. Sound familiar? Your brain is growing up too!
p: During adolescence, feelings can change quickly. Mood swings are common and normal.
Teenagers want more independence and care a lot about what friends think.
Peer pressure is when friends push you to do something. Good friends respect your 'no'.
Say no to tobacco, alcohol and drugs. They harm the growing body and brain.
When worried or sad, talk to a trusted adult: a parent, a teacher or a school counsellor. Hobbies, exercise, enough sleep and time with family also help.

ex.q: Some older students tell Rohan that he will be 'cool' if he tries chewing gutkha. What should he do?
st: Gutkha contains tobacco, which is harmful and addictive.
Real friends do not force you to do harmful things.
He can say 'no' firmly, walk away, and tell a trusted adult.
ex.a: He should say no firmly, move away from the group and talk to a trusted adult.

topics.rl: Many schools have counsellors and wellness clubs so students can talk about stress, exams and friendships.

topics.h: Stir hot chai with a steel spoon and soon the handle feels hot, even though it never touched the tea. How did the heat travel up?
p: Heat always flows from a hotter object or part to a colder one.
In conduction, heat passes from particle to particle through a material, while the material itself stays in place. It is the main way heat moves through solids.
Materials that let heat pass easily are good conductors of heat, such as metals like steel, copper and aluminium.
Materials that do not let heat pass easily are poor conductors (insulators), such as wood, plastic, cloth, wool and air.
Woollen clothes keep us warm because wool traps air between its fibres, and air is a poor conductor of heat.

ex.q: On a cold morning, an iron gate feels much colder than a wooden bench, though both are in the same place. Why?
st: Both are at about the same temperature because they are in the same air.
Iron is a good conductor, so it quickly takes heat away from your warm hand.
Wood is a poor conductor, so heat leaves your hand slowly.
ex.a: Iron conducts heat away from the hand faster, so it feels colder, even though both are at about the same temperature.

topics.rl: Steel kadhai with wooden or plastic handles, tea cosies, quilts (razai) and thermos flasks all use good and poor conductors smartly.

rv.summary: Heat always flows from hotter to colder. In conduction it passes from particle to particle while the material stays in place, mainly in solids. Metals are good conductors; wood, plastic, wool and air are poor conductors.

topics.h: Why do kitchen exhaust fans and ventilators sit high up near the ceiling, and how does the Sun's heat cross empty space to reach us?
p: In liquids and gases, heat moves mainly by convection: the warmer part becomes lighter and rises, and the cooler, heavier part moves down to take its place.
This up-and-down movement is called a convection current. You can see it when water is heated in a pan.
Radiation is the transfer of heat without needing any material in between. Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth through empty space by radiation.
We also feel radiation as warmth when we sit in front of a fire or a heater.
Dark-coloured surfaces absorb more heat; light-coloured surfaces reflect more. That is why white or light-coloured cotton clothes are comfortable in summer.

ex.q: A room heater is placed on the floor, but an air conditioner is fixed high on the wall. Why?
st: Warm air is lighter and rises, so warm air from a low heater spreads upward through the room.
Cool air is heavier and sinks, so cool air from a high AC spreads downward through the room.
Both placements use convection currents to mix the air in the whole room.
ex.a: Because warm air rises and cool air sinks, so these positions spread the heat or cool air through the room by convection.

topics.rl: Solar water heaters on rooftops have black panels to absorb the Sun's radiation, and many houses in Rajasthan are painted in light colours to stay cooler.

rv.summary: In liquids and gases heat moves by convection: warm parts rise and cooler parts sink, making convection currents. Radiation carries heat without any material, like heat from the Sun. Dark surfaces absorb more heat.

topics.h: At Marina Beach in Chennai, the breeze on a sunny afternoon comes from the sea. Late at night, it can come from the land. Why does it switch?
p: Land heats up faster than water during the day, and cools down faster at night.
Sea breeze (daytime): air above the hot land warms and rises. Cooler air from over the sea moves in to take its place, so wind blows from sea to land.
Land breeze (night): land becomes cooler than the sea. Air above the warmer sea rises, and cooler air from the land moves out to the sea.
Breezes are convection currents on a large scale: warm air rises and cooler air flows in.
These breezes make coastal places like Mumbai, Chennai and Kochi more pleasant.

ex.q: It is 2 p.m. on a sunny day in Goa. Which way is the breeze blowing, and why?
st: During the day, land heats up faster than the sea.
Warm air over the land rises.
Cooler air from the sea rushes in to replace it.
ex.a: From the sea towards the land: a sea breeze.

topics.rl: In the past, many fishermen sailed out early in the morning, helped by the land breeze, and came back later in the day with the sea breeze.

rv.summary: Land heats and cools faster than water. In the day a sea breeze blows from sea to land; at night a land breeze blows from land to sea. These breezes are convection currents.

topics.h: At Jantar Mantar in Jaipur stands a giant sundial, the Samrat Yantra, built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II. Its shadow tells the time!
p: Long ago, people measured time using the Sun and natural events: the day, the phases of the Moon and the year.
Sundials use a moving shadow; sand clocks (hourglasses) use falling sand; water clocks, called ghatika in ancient India, used a bowl with a small hole that slowly filled and sank in water.
A simple pendulum is a small heavy ball (bob) hanging from a thread. One complete to-and-fro swing is one oscillation, and the time it takes is the time period.
For a pendulum of fixed length at a place, the time period stays the same. A longer thread gives a longer time period. That is why pendulums were used in clocks.
The basic (SI) unit of time is the second (s). 1 minute = 60 s, 1 hour = 60 minutes = 3600 s, and 1 day = 24 hours.

ex.q: A pendulum makes 20 complete oscillations in 40 seconds. What is its time period?
st: Time period = total time ÷ number of oscillations
ex.a: 2 seconds

topics.rl: Today quartz watches and phones keep time very accurately, and atomic clocks, the most accurate of all, help satellites and GPS work.

rv.summary: People first measured time with the Sun and nature, then with sundials, sand clocks and water clocks (ghatika). A pendulum of fixed length has a constant time period, so it is used in clocks. The SI unit of time is the second.

topics.h: A cheetah can sprint faster than a car on a city road, but a tortoise is happy to take its time. How do we compare how fast things move?
p: Speed tells us how much distance is covered in a unit of time.
Speed = distance covered ÷ time taken.
The SI unit of speed is metre per second (m/s). For vehicles we often use kilometre per hour (km/h).
If an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time along a straight line, its motion is uniform. Otherwise it is non-uniform, like a bus in city traffic.
For non-uniform motion we use average speed = total distance ÷ total time. A speedometer shows a vehicle's speed and an odometer shows the distance travelled.

ex.q: A train travels 240 km from one city to another in 4 hours. What is its average speed in km/h?
st: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time
= 60 km/h
ex.a: 60 km/h

topics.rl: Road signs on highways show speed limits in km/h, and the Vande Bharat trains are known for their high speeds.

topics.h: A picture can tell a whole journey story! A distance-time graph shows at a glance whether someone was fast, slow or resting.
p: A distance-time graph shows time on the horizontal (x) axis and distance on the vertical (y) axis.
A straight sloping line means equal distance in equal time: uniform speed.
A steeper line means a higher speed: more distance in the same time.
A flat (horizontal) line means the distance is not changing: the object is at rest.
A curved line means the speed is changing: non-uniform motion.

ex.q: Neha cycles to school. Her graph rises steadily for 10 minutes, stays flat for 5 minutes, then rises steadily again. What happened?
st: Rising steadily means she was moving at a steady speed.
A flat part means her distance did not change: she was stopped.
Then the line rises again, so she started moving again.
ex.a: She cycled at a steady speed, stopped for 5 minutes (perhaps at a signal), then cycled again.

topics.rl: Delivery apps and fitness bands track your distance over time and draw graphs like this to show your speed and rest breaks.

topics.h: Chew a bite of roti for a long time and it starts tasting a little sweet. Your saliva is already doing chemistry!
p: Digestion breaks food down into simple substances that the body can absorb and use.
The path of food: mouth → food pipe (oesophagus) → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.
In the mouth, teeth break food into small pieces and saliva starts turning starch into sugar. Incisors cut, canines tear, and premolars and molars grind.

The stomach makes acid and digestive juices; the liver makes bile; the pancreas sends juices to the small intestine, where digestion is completed. Finger-like villi in the small intestine absorb the digested food into the blood.

The large intestine absorbs water and some salts from the undigested food. The waste leaves through the anus. Cows and buffaloes (ruminants) swallow grass quickly and later bring it back to chew as cud.

ex.q: Why does a roti taste sweet if you chew it slowly for a minute?
st: Roti is rich in starch.
Saliva contains a substance that breaks starch down into sugar.
Sugar tastes sweet, so the roti starts tasting sweet.
ex.a: Saliva changes some of the starch in the roti into sugar.

topics.rl: Doctors tell us to chew food well and eat fibre-rich food like fruits, vegetables and whole grains, so the digestive system works smoothly.

topics.h: Run up the stairs and you start huffing and puffing. Why does your body suddenly want so much more air?
p: Breathing means taking in air (inhaling) and giving out air (exhaling) through the nose and lungs.
Respiration is the process in the cells where food (glucose) is broken down using oxygen to release energy. Carbon dioxide and water are formed.
When we inhale, the diaphragm (a sheet of muscle below the lungs) moves down and the chest expands. When we exhale, it moves up and the chest becomes smaller.
During hard exercise, muscles may not get enough oxygen. Then they break down glucose without oxygen and form lactic acid, which can cause cramps.
Other animals breathe differently: fish use gills, earthworms breathe through their moist skin, insects have tiny holes called spiracles, and frogs use lungs and their moist skin.

ex.q: Air you breathe out is bubbled through lime water using a straw, and it turns milky faster than when fresh air is pumped through. What does this show?
st: Lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide.
Breathed-out air makes it milky faster.
So breathed-out air has more carbon dioxide.
ex.a: Exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than the air we breathe in.

topics.rl: Yoga breathing (pranayama) helps people breathe slowly and deeply. Athletes train to help their bodies use oxygen better.

rv.summary: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration in cells breaks down glucose with oxygen to release energy, making carbon dioxide and water. Without enough oxygen, muscles make lactic acid.

topics.h: Your heart is about the size of your fist, yet it beats again and again every minute of your life without taking a holiday!
p: Blood carries oxygen, digested food and other useful things to every part of the body, and takes away wastes like carbon dioxide.
The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood. The human heart has four chambers.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins bring blood back to the heart. Tiny tubes called capillaries connect them.
Blood has red blood cells (carry oxygen; their red pigment is haemoglobin), white blood cells (fight germs) and platelets (help blood clot), floating in a liquid called plasma.
Each heartbeat sends a push of blood through the arteries. We can feel this as the pulse at the wrist or neck. Doctors listen to the heart with a stethoscope.

ex.q: Ali counts his pulse while sitting, then again after skipping for two minutes. The second count is higher. Why?
st: Skipping makes the muscles work harder.
Working muscles need more oxygen and food.
The heart beats faster to deliver blood more quickly, so the pulse rises.
ex.a: His heart beats faster after exercise to send more oxygen-rich blood to his muscles.

topics.rl: Blood donation camps in India collect blood that can save lives in hospitals. Healthy adults can donate blood safely.

rv.summary: Blood carries oxygen and food to all body parts and removes wastes. The four-chambered heart pumps blood through arteries, capillaries and veins.

topics.h: A tiny neem seedling grows into a huge tree without eating a single meal. Where does all that food come from?
p: Green plants make their own food. This process is called photosynthesis.
Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using sunlight and the green pigment chlorophyll.
Leaves are the food factories of the plant. Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves through tiny pores called stomata.
The glucose made is used for energy and growth, and extra food is stored as starch.
Iodine solution turns blue-black when it touches starch, so it can show which leaves made food. (Leaf testing involves hot alcohol, so it is done only by a teacher.)

ex.q: One potted plant is kept in sunlight and an identical one in a dark cupboard for two days. A teacher tests a leaf from each with iodine. Which turns blue-black and why?
st: Photosynthesis needs sunlight.
Only the plant in sunlight could make food and store it as starch.
Iodine turns blue-black where starch is present.
ex.a: The leaf from the plant in sunlight turns blue-black, because only it made starch by photosynthesis.

topics.rl: Almost all the food we eat, from rice and wheat to mangoes and dal, comes from plants that made it by photosynthesis. Plants also release the oxygen we breathe.

rv.summary: Green plants make their own food by photosynthesis: carbon dioxide and water form glucose and oxygen using sunlight and chlorophyll. Leaves are the food factories, and extra food is stored as starch.

topics.h: Water climbs all the way to the top of a tall coconut tree without any pump. How does it get up there?
p: Roots absorb water and minerals from the soil, mainly through tiny root hairs.
Xylem is a set of tubes that carries water and minerals from the roots up to the stem, leaves and flowers.
Phloem is another set of tubes that carries food made in the leaves to all parts of the plant.
Plants lose water as vapour through stomata. This is called transpiration.
Transpiration creates a pull that helps draw water up through the xylem. It also cools the plant.

ex.q: A white flower with its stem kept in water with a few drops of red ink turns pinkish after a few hours. What does this show?
st: The coloured water was taken up by the stem.
It travelled upwards to the petals.
Water moves up through the xylem tubes.
ex.a: Water travels up the stem through the xylem to the flower.

topics.rl: Gardeners water the soil near the roots, not the leaves, because roots absorb water. On hot days, trees cool the air around them partly through transpiration.

rv.summary: Roots absorb water and minerals through root hairs. Xylem carries water and minerals up; phloem carries food from the leaves to all parts. Transpiration is water loss from leaves, which pulls water up and cools the plant.

topics.h: Plants make oxygen, so do they ever need oxygen themselves? Surprise: yes, all day and all night!
p: Like animals, plants respire: they break down food using oxygen to release energy, giving out carbon dioxide.
Every living part of a plant (roots, stems, leaves, flowers, seeds) respires, day and night.
Leaves take in air through stomata. Roots take oxygen from the air in the spaces between soil particles.
Over-watering fills these spaces with water, so roots cannot get enough air and the plant may die.
In daylight, photosynthesis makes more oxygen than the plant uses, so plants give out oxygen. At night, with no photosynthesis, plants only respire and give out carbon dioxide.

ex.q: Sprouting moong seeds are kept in a closed flask. After a day, the air from the flask turns lime water milky, and the flask feels slightly warm. What is happening?
st: Lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide.
The sprouting seeds are alive and respiring.
Respiration gives out carbon dioxide and releases energy, some as heat.
ex.a: The germinating seeds are respiring, giving out carbon dioxide and heat.

topics.rl: Mangrove trees in the Sundarbans grow in waterlogged mud, so some of their roots grow upwards out of the mud to take in air.

topics.h: Your shadow follows you everywhere, but it is short at noon and super-long in the evening. Why does it keep changing size?
p: Light travels in a straight line. That is why we cannot see around a corner.

Transparent materials (clear glass, clean water) let almost all light through. Translucent ones (butter paper, frosted glass) let some light through. Opaque ones (wood, cardboard, your body) let no light through.
A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light. We need a light source, an opaque object and a surface (screen) to see a shadow.
A shadow is dark whatever the colour of the object. Its size depends on how near the object is to the light: closer to the light gives a bigger shadow.
A pinhole camera shows that light travels in straight lines: the image it forms on its screen is upside down.

ex.q: During shadow-puppet play, Arjun moves his hand closer to the torch. What happens to the shadow on the wall?
st: The torch spreads light outwards in straight lines.
When the hand is closer to the torch, it blocks a wider part of the spreading light.
So a bigger area of the wall gets no light.
ex.a: The shadow becomes bigger.

topics.rl: Shadow puppetry, like Tholu Bommalata of Andhra Pradesh and Togalu Gombeyaata of Karnataka, uses light and shadows to tell stories.

topics.h: You can see this page only because light bounces off it into your eyes. That bounce has a name!
p: Reflection is the bouncing back of light when it falls on a surface. Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors reflect light very well.
The ray that falls on the mirror is the incident ray; the ray that bounces off is the reflected ray. The normal is an imaginary line at 90° to the mirror at the point where the ray hits.
The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
Law 1: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Law 2: the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane (on the same flat surface).

ex.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror making an angle of 30° with the mirror's surface. What are the angles of incidence and reflection?
st: The normal is at 90° to the mirror.
Angle of incidence = 90° − 30° = 60° (measured from the normal, not the mirror).
Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 60°.
ex.a: Both are 60°.

topics.rl: Bicycles have reflectors that shine when car lights fall on them at night, and road signs are made with reflective paint for safety.

rv.summary: Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal, and the incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in the same plane.
