topics.h: Why is the word AMBULANCE written backwards on the front of ambulances? Look in a mirror and find out!
p: A plane (flat) mirror forms an image that is upright (erect) and the same size as the object.
The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.
The image is laterally inverted: left and right appear swapped. Your right hand looks like the image's left hand.
The image in a plane mirror cannot be caught on a screen; it is a virtual image.

Curved mirrors: a concave mirror curves inwards (like the inside of a steel spoon) and is used by dentists and in torch reflectors. A convex mirror bulges outwards and gives a wider view, so it is used as the side mirror on vehicles.

ex.q: Priya stands 3 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is she from her image?
st: Her image is as far behind the mirror as she is in front: 3 m.
Distance from Priya to the image = 3 m + 3 m.
ex.a: 6 m

topics.rl: Periscopes use two plane mirrors to see over walls, kaleidoscopes use mirror strips to make patterns, and convex mirrors are placed at sharp mountain-road bends to show oncoming traffic.

rv.summary: A plane mirror gives an upright, same-size, virtual image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, with left and right swapped. Concave mirrors curve inwards and convex mirrors bulge outwards.
focus: Features of a plane mirror image
Lateral inversion and the 'AMBULANCE' sign
Uses of concave and convex mirrors
How a periscope works
remember: Plane mirror image: upright, same size, virtual, laterally inverted
Image distance behind = object distance in front
Concave (curves in): dentists, torch reflectors
Convex (bulges out): wider view, vehicle side mirrors
traps: The distance between you and your image is double your distance from the mirror.
A plane mirror image cannot be caught on a screen.
Don't mix up concave and convex uses.

topics.t: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
topics.h: Right now you are spinning with the Earth and also racing around the Sun, yet you feel perfectly still!
p: The Earth spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles. This spinning is called rotation.
The Earth rotates from west to east, once in about 24 hours. Rotation causes day and night, and makes the Sun appear to rise in the east and set in the west.
The Earth also moves around the Sun in a fixed path called its orbit. This is revolution, and one revolution takes about 365¼ days, which is one year.
The extra quarter days add up, so usually every fourth year has an extra day, 29 February. Such a year has 366 days and is called a leap year.
The Earth's axis is tilted. This tilt, along with revolution, gives us seasons. The Indian astronomer Aryabhata, about 1,500 years ago, wrote that the Earth rotates on its axis.

ex.q: Why does the Sun appear to rise in the east every morning?
st: The Earth rotates from west to east.
So places on the Earth turn towards the Sun from the eastern side first.
To us standing on the ground, the Sun seems to come up from the east.
ex.a: Because the Earth rotates from west to east, the Sun appears to rise in the east.

topics.rl: When it is morning in India, it is evening or night in the USA, because only half of the rotating Earth faces the Sun at a time.

rv.summary: The Earth rotates on its axis from west to east once in about 24 hours, causing day and night. It revolves around the Sun once in about 365¼ days, so every fourth year is usually a 366-day leap year.
focus: Rotation vs revolution
Effects of rotation: day and night, Sun rising in the east
Leap years and why they exist
Tilt of the axis and seasons; Aryabhata
remember: Rotation: west to east, about 24 hours → day and night
Revolution: about 365¼ days → one year
Leap year = 366 days, with 29 February
Aryabhata wrote that the Earth rotates on its axis
traps: Don't mix up rotation (spinning) and revolution (going around the Sun).
The Earth rotates west to east, so the Sun appears to move east to west.

topics.h: Diwali is celebrated on a moonless night (amavasya), while many festivals fall on full moon nights (purnima). The Moon has been India's calendar for ages!
p: The Moon does not make its own light. It shines because it reflects sunlight.
Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon goes around the Earth, we see different amounts of this lit half. These shapes are the phases of the Moon.
New moon (amavasya): the lit half faces away from us, so we cannot see the Moon. Full moon (purnima): we see the whole lit half as a bright disc.
After the new moon the visible part grows (waxing, called Shukla Paksha); after the full moon it shrinks (waning, called Krishna Paksha).
One full cycle of phases takes about 29½ days. The same side of the Moon always faces the Earth.

ex.q: Why can't we see the Moon on a new moon night even though it is in the sky?
st: The Moon shines only by reflecting sunlight.
On new moon day the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun.
Its lit side faces the Sun, and its dark side faces us.
ex.a: Because the side of the Moon facing us is not lit by the Sun.

topics.rl: Many Indian calendars and festivals follow the phases of the Moon, and fishermen watch the Moon because tides are stronger near new moon and full moon.

rv.summary: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight. As it goes around the Earth, we see different amounts of its lit half, giving phases from new moon to full moon and back in about 29½ days.
focus: Why the Moon shines and shows phases
New moon, full moon, waxing and waning
Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha
Why we always see the same face
remember: New moon (amavasya): not visible; full moon (purnima): bright full disc
Waxing (Shukla Paksha): new → full; waning (Krishna Paksha): full → new
One cycle of phases ≈ 29½ days
The same side of the Moon always faces the Earth
traps: The Moon does not change shape; we see different parts of its lit half.
Phases are not caused by the Earth's shadow.
Don't swap Shukla and Krishna Paksha.

topics.h: Imagine the Sun going dark in the middle of the day! A total solar eclipse makes birds settle as if it were dusk, but it lasts only a few minutes.
p: An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and Moon come in a straight line and one casts a shadow on the other.
Solar eclipse: the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth, and the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth. It can happen only on a new moon day.
Lunar eclipse: the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, and the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. It can happen only on a full moon night. In a total lunar eclipse the Moon often looks reddish.
Eclipses do not happen every month, because the Moon's path is slightly tilted compared to the Earth's path, so the three usually do not line up exactly.
Safety: never look at the Sun directly, even during a solar eclipse. Use proper certified solar eclipse glasses. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with bare eyes.

ex.q: Why can a solar eclipse happen only on a new moon day?
st: In a solar eclipse the Moon must be between the Sun and the Earth.
The Moon is between the Sun and the Earth only around new moon.
So the Moon's shadow can fall on the Earth only then.
ex.a: Because only at new moon is the Moon between the Sun and the Earth.

topics.rl: Scientists in India travel to places in the path of a total solar eclipse to study the Sun's outer layer, which is visible only when the Moon blocks the bright disc.

rv.summary: An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up. In a solar eclipse the Moon is in the middle (only at new moon); in a lunar eclipse the Earth is in the middle (only at full moon).
focus: Order of bodies in solar and lunar eclipses
Which phase each eclipse needs
Why eclipses do not happen every month
Safe viewing
remember: Solar eclipse: Sun – Moon – Earth; Moon's shadow on Earth; new moon only
Lunar eclipse: Sun – Earth – Moon; Earth's shadow on Moon; full moon only
The Moon's path is slightly tilted, so eclipses are not monthly
Watch a solar eclipse only with certified solar eclipse glasses
traps: Ordinary sunglasses are not safe for a solar eclipse.
Don't mix up which shadow falls where.
A lunar eclipse cannot happen on a new moon.

qa.q: What makes scientists change an accepted idea?
qa.e: Scientific ideas stand or fall on evidence. When careful new observations or experiments disagree with an idea, it is improved.

qa.q: Which tool first let people see the craters on the Moon and the moons of Jupiter?
qa.e: A telescope makes far-away objects look nearer and larger. Galileo used one to see the Moon's craters and moons going around Jupiter.

qa.q: Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork under a microscope. What did he discover?
qa.e: In 1665 Hooke saw small boxes in cork and called them 'cells'. This opened up the study of the tiny units of life.

qa.q: Long ago, many people believed that the Sun goes around the Earth. What do we know now?
qa.a: The Earth goes around the Sun
qa.e: Careful observations showed that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun. The Sun only seems to move because the Earth spins.

qa.q: Pluto is now called a dwarf planet. What does this example show about science?
qa.a: Scientists update how they group things as they learn more
qa.e: Pluto did not change. As astronomers found many similar objects, they made clearer rules for what counts as a planet.

qa.q: Which statement about science is correct?
qa.a: Science is a process that keeps growing
qa.e: Science is a way of finding out. It grows as people ask new questions and test them.

qa.q: Why do scientists share their results with other scientists?
qa.a: So others can check and repeat the work
qa.e: Other scientists repeating an experiment and getting the same result makes us more confident it is right.

qa.q: Earlier, people thought heavy and light objects always fall at very different speeds. Experiments showed that, without air in the way, they fall together. This shows that:
qa.a: Testing can correct a common belief
qa.e: A careful test showed that air resistance, not weight, causes most of the difference. The old belief was corrected by evidence.

qa.q: On which date is National Science Day celebrated in India?
qa.e: It marks the day in 1928 when C.V. Raman announced the discovery of the Raman effect.

qa.q: In which year did C.V. Raman win the Nobel Prize in Physics?
qa.e: He discovered the Raman effect in 1928 and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.

qa.q: What did Jagadish Chandra Bose's crescograph measure?
qa.a: The very small growth of plants
qa.e: The crescograph magnified tiny movements, showing how plants grow and respond to things around them.

qa.q: Who is known as the 'Birdman of India'?
qa.e: Salim Ali spent his life studying and writing about the birds of India.

qa.q: Chandrayaan-3's lander touched down near the Moon's south pole on which date?
qa.e: Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 and landed on 23 August 2023. India now marks 23 August as National Space Day.

qa.q: Edward Jenner is remembered for which discovery?
qa.e: In 1796 Jenner showed that a mild cowpox infection could protect people from smallpox. This was the start of vaccines.

qa.q: Why is it said that science is built 'on the shoulders' of earlier scientists?
qa.a: Each discovery uses knowledge found earlier
qa.e: New discoveries use tools, facts and ideas worked out earlier by others. Science is a chain of shared work.

qa.q: A big Moon mission needs experts in rockets, fuel, computers and maths. What does this show?
qa.a: Big science needs teamwork across subjects
qa.e: Rockets need physics, fuel needs chemistry, the path needs maths and control needs computers. Teams combine all of these.

qa.q: What is a hypothesis?
qa.a: A guess that can be tested
qa.e: A hypothesis is an idea you can test, such as 'Plants kept in sunlight will grow taller'. The experiment checks it.

qa.q: Arjun tests whether sunlight helps plants grow. Which is the ONE thing he should change?
qa.e: In a fair test you change only the factor you are testing. Water, pot and plant type must stay the same.

qa.q: In an experiment the result is different from what you predicted. What should you do?
qa.a: Record the real result and think about why
qa.e: Honest recording is the heart of science. Surprising results often lead to new discoveries.

qa.q: Why should an experiment be repeated a few times?
qa.a: To check that the result was not just luck
qa.e: If you get the same result again and again, you can be more confident it is real.

qa.q: Which question can be answered by a science experiment?
qa.a: Does salt water freeze at a lower temperature than plain water?
qa.e: Freezing temperature can be measured. The other questions are about likes and opinions.

qa.q: Riya notices ants walking in a line to a sugar spill. This first step of inquiry is called:
qa.e: Noticing something carefully with your senses is observation. It usually comes first and leads to a question.

qa.q: Kabir drops a paper ball and a flat sheet of paper from the same height at the same time. What is the fair-test idea here?
qa.a: Same paper and same height; only the shape is changed
qa.e: Keeping the paper and height the same means only the shape can explain any difference in falling time.

qa.q: Which of these is a conclusion?
qa.a: Plants kept in sunlight grew taller than those kept in a dark cupboard
qa.e: A conclusion states what the results show. The other options are a question, a plan and a list of materials.

qa.q: Which acid is found in curd?
qa.e: Bacteria turn milk into curd and make lactic acid, which gives curd its sour taste.

qa.q: Vinegar, used in pickles and salads, contains mainly which acid?
qa.e: Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid in water.

qa.q: How do bases usually feel when touched (when diluted and safe)?
qa.e: Bases feel soapy. 'Sour' is a taste, not a feel, and it belongs to acids.

qa.q: Which of these is a neutral substance?
qa.e: Sugar solution does not change the colour of litmus, so it is neutral. Lemon juice is acidic; soap and lime water are basic.

qa.q: Amla is a rich source of vitamin C. What is the chemical name of vitamin C?
qa.e: Vitamin C is ascorbic acid. It is found in amla, oranges, guava and many fruits.

qa.q: Why should you never taste chemicals in a science lab to find out if they are acids?
qa.a: Some acids and bases can burn or poison you
qa.e: Strong acids and bases can harm the mouth and skin. Scientists use indicators instead of tasting.

qa.q: Lime water is made by dissolving which substance in water?
qa.e: Lime water is a solution of calcium hydroxide. It is a base.

qa.q: Which pair has one acid and one base?
qa.e: Lemon juice is acidic and soap solution is basic. Vinegar and curd are both acids; soap and lime water are both bases; salt and sugar solutions are neutral.

qa.q: What colour does blue litmus turn in lemon juice?
qa.e: Lemon juice is acidic, and acids turn blue litmus red.

qa.q: A solution turns turmeric paper red. The solution is:
qa.e: Turmeric changes from yellow to red only in bases.

qa.q: Litmus is obtained from:
qa.e: Litmus dye comes from lichens. Rose and turmeric give other natural indicators.

qa.q: Salt solution is tested with red and blue litmus. What happens?
qa.e: Common salt solution is neutral, so it changes neither red nor blue litmus.

qa.q: China rose extract is added to vinegar. What colour appears?
qa.e: Vinegar is acidic. China rose indicator turns dark pink (magenta) in acids and green in bases.

qa.q: Why is red litmus alone not enough to tell an acid from a neutral solution?
qa.a: Red litmus stays red in both
qa.e: Red litmus changes only in a base. To spot an acid you need blue litmus, which turns red in acids.

qa.q: What is an indicator?
qa.a: A substance that changes colour in acids or bases
qa.e: Indicators show whether a substance is acidic, basic or neutral by their colour change.

qa.q: Which of these would turn red litmus blue?
qa.e: Baking soda solution is basic, and bases turn red litmus blue. Orange juice and vinegar are acids; sugar solution is neutral.

qa.q: What are the products when an acid reacts with a base?
qa.e: Neutralisation forms a salt and water, and heat is also given out.

qa.q: Milk of magnesia is taken for acidity. It works because it is:
qa.a: A base that neutralises extra stomach acid
qa.e: Milk of magnesia contains magnesium hydroxide, a base. It neutralises extra acid in the stomach.

qa.q: An ant sting contains which acid?
qa.e: Ants inject formic acid, which causes the burning feeling.

qa.q: Which is used to treat an ant bite?
qa.e: Baking soda is a mild base and neutralises the formic acid. Vinegar, lemon and tamarind are acids and would not help.

qa.q: During neutralisation, the test tube becomes slightly warm. Why?
qa.a: Heat is given out in the reaction
qa.e: Neutralisation releases heat, so the mixture warms up.

qa.q: Soil in a field is too basic. What should the farmer add?
qa.e: Compost releases acids that neutralise the extra base. Quicklime, slaked lime and baking soda are bases and would make it worse.

qa.q: Why must factories treat acidic waste before releasing it into rivers?
qa.a: The acid can harm fish and plants in the water
qa.e: Acidic waste harms living things in water. Adding a base neutralises it first.

qa.q: In science, the word 'salt' in 'acid + base gives salt + water' means:
qa.a: A new substance formed from the acid and base
qa.e: Different acids and bases form different salts. Common salt (sodium chloride) is just one of them.

qa.q: Which part of a torch bulb glows?
qa.e: The filament is a thin coiled wire that becomes hot and glows when current passes through it.

qa.q: What is the metal cap on top of a cell called?
qa.e: The metal cap is the positive (+) terminal. The flat metal disc at the bottom is the negative (−) terminal.

qa.q: Where does a torch cell (dry cell) get its electricity from?
qa.e: A cell turns stored chemical energy into electricity. When these chemicals are used up, the cell has to be replaced or recharged.

qa.q: An LED does not glow even though the cell is new. What is the most likely reason?
qa.a: It is connected the wrong way round
qa.e: An LED glows only when its longer leg is connected towards the positive terminal. Turning it around fixes the problem.

qa.q: What is a battery?
qa.a: Two or more cells joined together
qa.e: In a battery the positive terminal of one cell is joined to the negative terminal of the next.

qa.q: What does a switch do in a circuit?
qa.a: It joins or breaks the path of electricity
qa.e: In the ON position the switch completes the path; in the OFF position it breaks it.

qa.q: Which of these is a safe habit?
qa.a: Never open, burn or play with cells
qa.e: Cells contain chemicals, and wall sockets carry dangerous electricity. Old cells should be given for proper disposal.

qa.q: Why does a torch stop glowing after being used for many weeks?
qa.a: The chemicals in its cells are used up
qa.e: As the cell works, its chemicals get used up. Then it can no longer push electricity through the bulb.

qa.q: What is a closed circuit?
qa.a: A complete path for electricity with no gaps
qa.e: Electricity flows only through a complete loop. 'Closed' means the loop has no gap.

qa.q: The switch in a circuit is OFF. What happens?
qa.a: The circuit is open and the bulb does not glow
qa.e: OFF means the switch has made a gap in the path, so no current flows.

qa.q: In the circuit symbol of a cell, which line shows the positive terminal?
qa.e: By agreement the longer thin line is positive (+) and the shorter thick line is negative (−).

qa.q: Why do we use symbols to draw circuits?
qa.a: They are quick to draw and understood everywhere
qa.e: Standard symbols let anyone, anywhere, read a circuit diagram without drawing real-looking pictures.

qa.q: A bulb's two wires are both connected to the negative terminal of a cell. Does it glow?
qa.a: No, because the circuit is not complete
qa.e: Electricity must go from one terminal through the bulb to the other terminal. Here the positive terminal is left out.

qa.q: In a working circuit, electricity is said to flow from:
qa.a: The positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal
qa.e: In circuit diagrams we show current leaving the positive terminal and returning to the negative terminal.

qa.q: Sana's bulb flickers when she shakes her circuit. What is the most likely cause?
qa.e: A loose wire keeps making and breaking the path, so the bulb flickers on and off.

qa.q: To make a bulb glow brighter in a torch, two cells are placed one after the other. How should they be joined?
qa.a: Positive terminal of one to negative terminal of the other
qa.e: Cells in a battery are joined + to −. If they face the same way like this, they work together.

qa.q: Which of these is a good conductor of electricity?
qa.e: Copper is a metal, and metals conduct electricity well. That is why most wires are made of copper.

qa.q: Which material is an insulator?
qa.e: Dry wood does not let electricity pass easily. Aluminium and iron are metals, and graphite conducts too.

qa.q: Why are electric wires covered with plastic?
qa.a: Plastic is an insulator and protects us from shocks
qa.e: The copper or aluminium inside carries the current. The plastic covering stops it from reaching our hands.

qa.q: Which non-metal conducts electricity?
qa.e: Graphite, a form of carbon found in pencil 'lead', conducts electricity although it is a non-metal.

qa.q: You touch the two free wires of a tester to a safety pin and the bulb glows. The safety pin is:
qa.e: The bulb glows because current passed through the pin. So the pin conducts electricity.

qa.q: Why is it dangerous to touch a switch with wet hands?
qa.a: Water on hands can let electricity pass into the body
qa.e: Ordinary water carries electricity easily enough to give a dangerous shock through wet skin.

qa.q: What is the mains supply voltage in Indian homes?
qa.e: Homes in India get about 230 volts, which can kill. A torch cell gives only about 1.5 volts, which is safe for experiments.

qa.q: An electrician's screwdriver has a plastic handle because:
qa.e: The insulating handle stops current from flowing into the electrician's hand.

qa.q: Aluminium can be beaten into thin foil. This property is called:
qa.e: Malleability is the ability to be beaten into thin sheets. Ductility is about drawing into wires.

qa.q: Copper is drawn into thin wires for electric cables. This property is called:
qa.e: Ductile metals can be pulled into thin wires without breaking.

qa.q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
qa.e: Mercury is a metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature. Other common metals are solids.

qa.q: Why are temple and school bells made of metal?
qa.a: Metals are sonorous and ring when struck
qa.e: Sonorous materials give a ringing sound when hit, which makes metals ideal for bells.

qa.q: Which metal is soft enough to be cut with a knife?
qa.e: Sodium (and potassium) are soft metals. Most other metals are hard.

qa.q: A freshly cut piece of metal looks shiny. This shine is called:
qa.e: The shiny look of metals is called metallic lustre. Metals can look dull when their surface gets coated by air and moisture over time.

qa.q: Cooking pans are usually made of metal because metals:
qa.e: Metals pass heat quickly from the flame to the food.

qa.q: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
qa.e: Silver conducts electricity best, with copper a close second. Copper is used more in wires because it is much cheaper.

qa.q: What happens when a lump of sulphur is hammered?
qa.a: It breaks into pieces or powder
qa.e: Sulphur is a non-metal, and solid non-metals are brittle.

qa.q: Which non-metal is a liquid at room temperature?
qa.e: Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid non-metal. Mercury is also a liquid, but it is a metal.

qa.q: Which non-metal is shiny (lustrous)?
qa.e: Iodine crystals are shiny, even though iodine is a non-metal.

qa.q: Sulphur burns to form sulphur dioxide, which dissolves in water. The solution:
qa.e: Oxides of non-metals form acidic solutions, and acids turn blue litmus red.

qa.q: The oxide formed when magnesium burns gives a solution that is:
qa.e: Magnesium is a metal. Metal oxides form basic solutions that turn red litmus blue.

qa.q: Diamond and graphite are both forms of which element?
qa.e: Both are made only of carbon atoms, joined in different ways. That is why they behave so differently.

qa.q: Which is true for most non-metals?
qa.a: They are poor conductors of heat and electricity
qa.e: Most non-metals are dull, brittle (if solid) and poor conductors. Many are gases.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-metal gas?
qa.e: Nitrogen is a non-metal and makes up most of the air. Sodium, zinc and mercury are metals.

qa.q: Why is aluminium used to make aeroplane parts?
qa.e: Aluminium is a light metal that can be made strong, which suits aeroplanes.

qa.q: Which non-metal is used to make fertilisers?
qa.e: Plants need nitrogen to grow. Fertilisers like urea contain nitrogen.

qa.q: Which substance is used to kill germs in drinking water?
qa.e: Small amounts of chlorine are added in water treatment plants to kill germs.

qa.q: Why are electric wires usually made of copper?
qa.a: Copper is ductile and a good conductor of electricity
qa.e: Copper can be drawn into wires (ductile) and carries current well.

qa.q: Silver vark on sweets is possible because silver is:
qa.e: Silver can be beaten into extremely thin sheets because it is highly malleable.

qa.q: Why is gold so popular for jewellery?
qa.a: It is lustrous, malleable and keeps its shine for a long time
qa.e: Gold reacts very little with air and water, so it does not lose its shine, and it can be shaped into fine designs.

qa.q: Which non-metal is used in pencils?
qa.a: Carbon in the form of graphite
qa.e: Despite the name 'pencil lead', the black core is graphite, a form of carbon, mixed with clay.

qa.q: Nitrogen is filled in chips packets because:
qa.a: It does not react with food and keeps it fresh
qa.e: Nitrogen is unreactive. It keeps oxygen out, so the chips do not go stale quickly and stay protected from crushing.

qa.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
qa.e: Cooking forms new substances with a new colour, taste and smell. The others change only shape or state.

qa.q: Which of these is a physical change?
qa.e: Melted butter is still butter and can become solid again. The others form new substances.

qa.q: Which sign usually tells us that a chemical change has happened?
qa.a: A new gas or a new colour appears
qa.e: Gas, colour change, heat or light and new smells are signs of new substances forming.

qa.q: Baking soda and vinegar fizz together. Which gas is formed?
qa.e: The fizz is carbon dioxide gas. It turns lime water milky.

qa.q: Carbon dioxide is passed through lime water. What do you see?
qa.e: Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water to form a white solid, calcium carbonate, which makes it look milky.

qa.q: Why is tearing paper a physical change even though it cannot be reversed?
qa.e: The pieces are still paper. A physical change is about no new substance, not about being reversible.

qa.q: When a candle burns, which part is a physical change?
qa.e: Melting wax only changes its state. Burning makes new substances like carbon dioxide and water vapour.

qa.q: Which of these changes is chemical?
qa.e: Bacteria change milk into curd, a new substance with a sour taste. The others form no new substance.

qa.q: What two things are needed for iron to rust?
qa.e: Iron reacts with oxygen from the air and water (moisture) to form rust.

qa.q: What colour is rust?
qa.e: Rust is a reddish-brown, flaky substance called iron oxide.

qa.q: Is rusting a physical or a chemical change?
qa.a: Chemical, because a new substance forms
qa.e: Rust is a new substance with different properties from iron.

qa.q: Galvanisation means coating iron with a layer of:
qa.e: In galvanisation a layer of zinc is put on iron. The zinc protects the iron from air and water.

qa.q: Why does iron rust faster in Mumbai or Chennai than in Jaipur?
qa.a: The air near the sea is moist and salty
qa.e: Coastal cities have humid, salty air. More moisture and salt speed up rusting.

qa.q: Why is a bicycle chain oiled?
qa.a: The oil keeps air and water away from the iron
qa.e: A layer of oil or grease blocks air and moisture, so rusting slows down.

qa.q: An iron nail is kept in boiled water with a layer of oil on top. Why does it not rust?
qa.e: Boiling removes dissolved air and the oil layer stops new air from dissolving. Without air, iron does not rust.

qa.q: Stainless steel does not rust easily because:
qa.a: Iron is mixed with metals like chromium and nickel
qa.e: Adding chromium and nickel to iron makes stainless steel, which resists rusting.

qa.q: What is crystallisation?
qa.a: Getting large, pure crystals of a substance from its solution
qa.e: In crystallisation a hot, strong solution is cooled slowly so pure crystals separate out.

qa.q: Why is hot water used to make the solution for crystallisation?
qa.a: More substance dissolves in hot water
qa.e: Hot water dissolves more. As it cools it cannot hold as much, so crystals form.

qa.q: Is crystallisation a physical or chemical change?
qa.e: The crystals are the same substance as before. Only the form changes.

qa.q: To get bigger crystals, the solution should be cooled:
qa.e: Slow, undisturbed cooling gives the crystals time to grow large.

qa.q: Salt from drying sea water is not pure because:
qa.a: Other dissolved substances are left behind with it
qa.e: Evaporation leaves all dissolved substances behind together. Crystallisation can separate pure salt.

qa.q: Which of these is made by crystallisation?
qa.e: Mishri is large sugar crystals grown from thick sugar syrup.

qa.q: Why is the hot solution filtered before cooling?
qa.e: Filtering removes dirt that did not dissolve, so the crystals come out clean.

qa.q: Which of these is commonly used to grow crystals in a school activity?
qa.e: Alum dissolves well in hot water and forms clear crystals as the solution cools. Flour does not dissolve, and milk and oil do not give crystals this way.

qa.q: What is adolescence?
qa.a: The stage of life between childhood and adulthood
qa.e: Adolescence covers the teenage years when a child grows into an adult.

qa.q: What controls the changes of puberty?
qa.e: Hormones are chemical messengers made by glands in the body. They start and guide the changes of puberty.

qa.q: A sudden increase in height during puberty is called:
qa.e: Many adolescents grow taller quickly over a short time. This is the growth spurt.

qa.q: Why does a boy's voice become deeper during puberty?
qa.e: The voice box (larynx) grows larger, which makes the voice deeper. It may crack for a while.

qa.q: Why do many teenagers get pimples?
qa.a: Oil glands in the skin become more active
qa.e: During puberty the skin makes more oil, which can block tiny pores and cause pimples.

qa.q: Riya's friend has begun her periods and is scared. What is correct?
qa.a: Periods are a normal, healthy part of growing up
qa.e: Menstruation is a natural monthly process in girls' bodies after puberty begins. She can talk to a trusted adult.

qa.q: Do all children begin puberty at the same age?
qa.a: No, the timing is different for each person
qa.e: Puberty can start earlier or later. Girls often start a little before boys.

qa.q: Which change happens to both boys and girls during puberty?
qa.a: New hair grows under the arms
qa.e: Underarm hair grows in both. A very deep voice and a beard are mostly seen in boys; periods happen in girls.

qa.q: Why should adolescents bathe every day?
qa.a: Sweat and oil increase, and germs can cause body odour
qa.e: Sweat glands work more during adolescence. Daily bathing keeps the skin clean and fresh.

qa.q: Which food is a good source of calcium?
qa.e: Milk, curd, paneer and ragi are rich in calcium, which builds strong bones.

qa.q: Iron in food helps the body to:
qa.e: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in blood.

qa.q: Which is the right thing to do about pimples?
qa.a: Wash the face gently and not squeeze them
qa.e: Squeezing can cause infection and marks. Gentle washing keeps pores clean.

qa.q: What is a correct practice during periods?
qa.a: Change sanitary pads or cloth regularly and throw used pads wrapped in a dustbin
qa.e: Changing regularly prevents infection. Wrapped disposal in a bin keeps surroundings clean.

qa.q: Which of these foods is rich in iron?
qa.e: Palak, methi, other green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates and pulses provide iron.

qa.q: Why is a balanced diet very important during adolescence?
qa.a: The body is growing fast and needs many nutrients
qa.e: Rapid growth needs proteins, vitamins, minerals and energy from a variety of foods.

qa.q: Which daily habit helps both the body and the mind stay healthy?
qa.e: Exercise builds strong muscles and bones and also lifts the mood.

qa.q: What are mood swings?
qa.e: In adolescence, feelings can change fast. This is common and usually settles with time.

qa.q: What is peer pressure?
qa.a: Feeling pushed by friends to do something
qa.e: Peers are people of your age group. Their push to act a certain way is peer pressure.

qa.q: Friends ask Tara to bunk class. What is a healthy response?
qa.e: Saying no to harmful choices shows confidence. Good friends will accept it.

qa.q: Who is a good person to talk to about worries?
qa.a: A trusted adult like a parent, teacher or counsellor
qa.e: Trusted adults can listen and help. Strangers online may not be safe.

qa.q: Why should adolescents avoid tobacco, alcohol and drugs?
qa.a: They harm the body and brain and are addictive
qa.e: These substances damage health and are hard to stop once started.

qa.q: Which activity can help reduce stress?
qa.a: Playing a sport or doing a hobby
qa.e: Exercise and hobbies relax the mind and improve mood.

qa.q: Why do teenagers often want more independence?
qa.a: It is a normal part of growing up
qa.e: Wanting to decide things for yourself is a natural part of becoming an adult.

qa.q: Ishaan feels sad for many days and does not want to play. What should he do?
qa.a: Talk to a trusted adult about it
qa.e: Sharing feelings with a parent, teacher or counsellor helps. They can find more help if needed.

qa.q: In which direction does heat flow?
qa.a: From a hotter object to a colder object
qa.e: Heat always moves from where it is hotter to where it is colder, until both reach the same temperature.

qa.q: Conduction is the main way heat travels through:
qa.e: In conduction heat passes from particle to particle, so it works best in solids.

qa.q: Why do cooking pans have wooden or plastic handles?
qa.a: Wood and plastic are poor conductors of heat
qa.e: Poor conductors do not let heat reach your hand, so you can hold the pan safely.

qa.q: Which is the best conductor of heat?
qa.e: Copper is a metal, and metals conduct heat well. Wood, wool and plastic are poor conductors.

qa.q: Why do woollen clothes keep us warm in winter?
qa.a: Wool traps air, which is a poor conductor of heat
qa.e: Trapped air slows down heat leaving our body. The clothes do not make heat themselves.

qa.q: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon are kept in hot dal. After a minute, which handle is hotter?
qa.e: Metal conducts heat quickly up the handle. Wood is a poor conductor, so its handle stays cooler.

qa.q: In conduction, what happens to the material itself?
qa.a: It stays in place while heat passes through it
qa.e: Particles pass on heat to their neighbours but do not travel. Moving material carries heat in convection, not conduction.

qa.q: Why does a steel glass of hot milk become hot all over?
qa.a: Steel conducts heat from the milk to the whole glass
qa.e: Heat from the milk passes through the steel by conduction, so the whole glass warms up.

qa.q: How does heat from the Sun reach the Earth?
qa.e: There is almost no material in space to carry heat by conduction or convection. Radiation can travel through empty space.

qa.q: In convection, why does heated water rise?
qa.a: It becomes lighter than the cooler water around it
qa.e: Warm water expands, becomes less dense (lighter for its size) and rises. Cooler water sinks to take its place.

qa.q: Convection happens in:
qa.e: Convection needs the material to move, and only liquids and gases can flow.

qa.q: Which colour of clothes keeps you cooler on a sunny summer day?
qa.e: Light colours reflect more of the Sun's heat, while dark colours absorb more.

qa.q: Ventilators in rooms are placed near the ceiling because:
qa.a: Warm air rises and can escape from there
qa.e: Warm air, being lighter, rises and goes out through the high ventilators, while fresh cooler air enters from below.

qa.q: You feel warm sitting in front of a bonfire even though the air between you is not very hot. This is mainly due to:
qa.e: Heat reaches you directly from the fire by radiation. Hot air from the fire mostly rises upward by convection.

qa.q: Why are solar cooker boxes painted black inside?
qa.e: Black absorbs more of the Sun's radiation, so the cooker gets hotter and cooks food.

qa.q: When water is heated in a pan, the moving loop of water is called a:
qa.e: Hot water rises and cool water sinks, forming a loop of moving water called a convection current.

qa.q: During a sunny day near the sea, which heats up faster?
qa.e: Land heats up faster than water, so the air above land becomes warmer in the day.

qa.q: What is a sea breeze?
qa.a: Wind blowing from the sea towards the land in the day
qa.e: In the day, warm air over land rises and cooler sea air flows in towards the land.

qa.q: When does a land breeze usually blow?
qa.e: At night the land cools faster than the sea, so cooler air flows from the land to the sea.

qa.q: Why does air above the land rise during the day?
qa.e: The hot land warms the air above it. Warm air is lighter, so it rises.

qa.q: At night, the sea is warmer than the land. What happens to the air above the sea?
qa.a: It rises, and air from the land moves in
qa.e: Air above the warmer sea rises, and cooler air from the land flows towards the sea. This is a land breeze.

qa.q: Land and sea breezes are an example of heat transfer by:
qa.e: Moving air carries heat: warm air rises and cooler air takes its place. That is convection.

qa.q: Why does land cool faster than sea water at night?
qa.a: Land loses heat faster than water
qa.e: Water takes longer to heat up and also longer to cool down, so at night the sea stays warmer than the land.

qa.q: Riya is on a beach in Puri in the afternoon. Where will a kite on a long string most likely drift?
qa.e: In the afternoon a sea breeze blows from the sea to the land, so the kite drifts towards the land.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of time?
qa.e: The second (s) is the standard unit of time used by scientists all over the world.

qa.q: What is the time period of a pendulum?
qa.a: Time taken for one complete oscillation
qa.e: One oscillation is a full to-and-fro swing, back to the starting point. The time for it is the time period.

qa.q: A pendulum completes 10 oscillations in 20 seconds. What is its time period?
qa.e: Time period = 20 s ÷ 10 = 2 s.

qa.q: How many seconds are there in 2 hours?
What happens to the time period of a pendulum if its thread is made longer?
qa.e: A longer pendulum takes more time to complete each swing.

qa.q: Which ancient Indian device measured time using a bowl with a small hole floating in water?
qa.e: The bowl slowly filled with water and sank after a fixed time, marking a unit of time.

qa.q: A sundial works because:
qa.a: The shadow of a stick moves as the Sun appears to move across the sky
qa.e: As the Earth rotates, the Sun seems to move, so the shadow moves across marked lines.

qa.q: How many minutes are there in 3 hours?
qa.e: 1 hour = 60 minutes, so 3 hours = 3 × 60 = 180 minutes.

qa.q: What is the formula for speed?
qa.e: Speed tells distance covered in each unit of time, so we divide distance by time.

qa.q: Which is the SI unit of speed?
qa.e: Speed is distance per time, so its SI unit is metre per second.

qa.q: A boy runs 200 m in 40 s. What is his speed in metres per second?
A bus travels at 50 km/h for 3 hours. How many kilometres does it cover?
qa.e: Distance = speed × time = 50 × 3 = 150 km.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of non-uniform motion?
qa.a: A car moving in heavy traffic
qa.e: In traffic the car keeps speeding up, slowing down and stopping, so it covers unequal distances in equal times.

qa.q: A car travels 120 km in 2 hours, but stops and starts on the way. Its average speed in km/h is:
qa.e: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 120 ÷ 2 = 60 km/h.

qa.q: Which instrument in a vehicle shows its speed?
qa.e: The speedometer shows speed. The odometer shows the total distance travelled.

qa.q: A scooter moves at 72 km/h. What is this speed in metres per second?
On a distance-time graph, what does a horizontal (flat) line show?
qa.e: If the distance stays the same as time passes, the object is not moving.

qa.q: What does a straight line sloping upward show?
qa.e: A straight sloping line means the same distance is covered in each equal time interval.

qa.q: Two cars' graphs are straight lines. Car A's line is steeper than car B's. Which is faster?
qa.e: A steeper line means more distance in the same time, which means a higher speed.

qa.q: A car's distance is 40 km after 1 hour, 80 km after 2 hours and 120 km after 3 hours. What is its speed in km/h?
qa.e: It covers 40 km in every hour, so its speed is 40 km/h and its graph is a straight line.

qa.q: A car covers 40 km in each hour for 3 hours. Its distance-time graph will be:
qa.e: Equal distances in equal times means uniform motion, which gives a straight sloping line.

qa.q: In a distance-time graph, what is shown on the vertical (y) axis?
qa.e: Distance goes up the vertical axis and time along the horizontal axis.

qa.q: Rahul walks 2 km in the first hour, rests for 1 hour, then walks 2 km more in the third hour. What is his total distance in km?
qa.e: He walked 2 km + 0 km + 2 km = 4 km. The rest hour adds no distance and shows as a flat part on the graph.

qa.q: A line on a distance-time graph gets steeper and steeper. The object is:
qa.e: A steeper slope means greater speed, so a line getting steeper shows increasing speed.

qa.q: Where does the digestion of food begin?
qa.e: Teeth break food and saliva starts digesting starch right in the mouth.

qa.q: Where is the digestion of food completed?
qa.e: Juices from the liver, pancreas and the intestine's own walls complete digestion in the small intestine.

qa.q: What is the main job of the villi?
qa.a: To absorb digested food into the blood
qa.e: Villi are tiny finger-like bumps that give a large surface for absorbing digested food.

qa.q: Which is the largest gland in the human body?
qa.e: The liver is the largest gland. It makes bile, which helps digest fats.

qa.q: Which pointed teeth are mainly used for tearing food?
qa.e: Canines are pointed teeth for tearing. Incisors cut and molars grind.

qa.q: How many permanent teeth does an adult usually have?
qa.e: An adult usually has 32 permanent teeth. Children have 20 milk teeth.

qa.q: What does the large intestine mainly absorb?
qa.e: Most digested food is absorbed in the small intestine. The large intestine takes back water and some salts.

qa.q: A cow is seen chewing even when she is not eating fresh grass. Why?
qa.a: She is chewing cud, food brought back from her rumen
qa.e: Ruminants like cows store swallowed grass in the rumen and later bring it back to the mouth to chew properly.

qa.q: What is released during respiration in our cells?
qa.e: Glucose is broken down using oxygen to release energy, along with carbon dioxide and water.

qa.q: Which gas do we need to take in for respiration?
qa.e: Cells use oxygen to break down glucose and release energy.

qa.q: What happens to the diaphragm when we breathe in?
qa.e: The diaphragm moves down and the ribs move up and out, so the chest becomes bigger and air flows in.

qa.q: Why do muscles sometimes get cramps after hard exercise?
qa.a: Lactic acid builds up when muscles get too little oxygen
qa.e: Without enough oxygen, muscles break glucose down without oxygen and form lactic acid, which causes cramps.

qa.q: How does a fish breathe in water?
qa.a: Using gills, which take oxygen dissolved in water
qa.e: Gills take in oxygen that is dissolved in the water.

qa.q: Which animal breathes through its moist skin?
qa.e: Earthworms have no lungs; gases pass through their moist skin.

qa.q: Why is breathing through the nose better than breathing through the mouth?
qa.a: Hairs and mucus in the nose trap dust and germs
qa.e: The nose cleans the air before it reaches the lungs.

qa.q: Dolphins live in water but come up to the surface often. Why?
qa.e: Dolphins are mammals with lungs, so they must come up to breathe air through a blowhole.

qa.q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
qa.e: The heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood through blood vessels.

qa.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
qa.e: Arteries take blood away from the heart; veins bring it back.

qa.q: What is the job of white blood cells?
qa.e: White blood cells protect the body by attacking germs.

qa.q: What gives blood its red colour?
qa.e: Haemoglobin is a red substance that also carries oxygen.

qa.q: When you get a small cut, the bleeding soon stops. Which part of blood helps?
qa.e: Platelets help form a clot that seals the cut.

qa.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
qa.e: The human heart has four chambers: two on top and two below.

qa.q: Why does your pulse rate go up after running?
qa.a: The heart beats faster to supply more oxygen
qa.e: Muscles need more oxygen during exercise, so the heart pumps faster.

qa.q: What are the tiny blood vessels that connect arteries and veins called?
qa.e: Capillaries are very thin vessels where oxygen and food pass from blood to the body's cells.

qa.q: What is the main raw material that plants take from the air for photosynthesis?
qa.e: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air through stomata and water from the soil.

qa.q: Which gas is given out during photosynthesis?
qa.e: Photosynthesis releases oxygen into the air, which animals and humans breathe.

qa.q: Why are leaves called the food factories of a plant?
qa.e: Leaves have chlorophyll and get sunlight, so most food is made in them.

qa.q: What is the role of chlorophyll?
qa.e: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that traps the Sun's energy for making food.

qa.q: In what form do plants store extra food?
qa.e: Glucose is changed into starch for storage, for example in potatoes and grains.

qa.q: Which test shows the presence of starch in a leaf?
qa.e: Iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch.

qa.q: A croton leaf has green and yellow patches. After a starch test, only the green parts turn blue-black. Why?
qa.a: Only the green parts have chlorophyll to make food
qa.e: Photosynthesis happens only where chlorophyll is present, so starch forms only in the green parts.

qa.q: Through which part do carbon dioxide and oxygen enter and leave a leaf?
qa.e: Stomata are tiny openings, mostly on the underside of leaves, that let gases in and out.

qa.q: Which tissue carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves?
qa.e: Xylem tubes carry water and dissolved minerals upwards.

qa.q: Which tissue carries food from the leaves to other parts of the plant?
qa.e: Phloem carries the food made in leaves to the stem, roots, fruits and other parts.

qa.q: What is transpiration?
qa.a: Loss of water as vapour from the leaves
qa.e: Water evaporates through the stomata of leaves. This is transpiration.

qa.q: How does transpiration help a plant?
qa.a: It helps pull water up and cools the plant
qa.e: As water evaporates from leaves, more water is pulled up from the roots. Evaporation also cools the leaves.

qa.q: Through which part do plants mostly absorb water?
qa.e: Root hairs give a large surface area to absorb water and minerals from the soil.

qa.q: A stem is placed in water with red ink. Where will the red colour be seen inside the stem?
qa.e: The coloured water rises through the xylem, so these tubes look red when the stem is cut.

qa.q: Why do plants need minerals from the soil?
qa.e: Minerals like nitrogen and potassium help plants grow and stay healthy.

qa.q: On a hot, sunny day, a plant loses more water through its leaves. This is because:
qa.e: Heat speeds up evaporation, so more water escapes from the stomata.

qa.q: When do plants respire?
qa.a: All the time, day and night
qa.e: All living cells need energy all the time, so plants respire both day and night.

qa.q: How do the roots of a plant get oxygen?
qa.a: From air in the spaces between soil particles
qa.e: Soil has tiny air spaces between particles, and roots take oxygen from there.

qa.q: Why can a potted plant die if it is watered too much?
qa.a: Water fills the air spaces and roots cannot get oxygen
qa.e: When the soil is waterlogged, roots cannot respire properly.

qa.q: What gas do germinating seeds give out?
qa.e: Sprouting seeds respire quickly and give out carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky.

qa.q: During the day, why do plants give out oxygen even though they are also respiring?
qa.a: Photosynthesis makes more oxygen than respiration uses
qa.e: Both processes happen in daylight, but photosynthesis is usually faster, so extra oxygen is released.

qa.q: Which process uses oxygen and releases energy from food?
qa.e: Respiration breaks down food using oxygen to release energy.

qa.q: Why do some mangrove trees have roots growing upwards out of the mud?
qa.a: To take in air, because the mud is waterlogged
qa.e: Waterlogged mud has little air, so these special roots grow upward to take in oxygen.

qa.q: Which of these does NOT respire?
qa.e: All living parts of a plant respire. Only dead parts, like a dry fallen stick, do not.

qa.q: A shadow is formed when light is blocked by:
qa.e: Opaque objects do not let light pass, so a dark region forms behind them.

qa.q: Which of these is translucent?
qa.e: Butter paper lets some light through but you cannot see clearly through it.

qa.q: What colour is the shadow of a green leaf in sunlight?
qa.e: A shadow is a region where light does not reach, so it is dark no matter the colour of the object.

qa.q: What does a pinhole camera show about light?
qa.e: Straight rays crossing at the pinhole make an upside-down image, which proves light travels straight.

qa.q: The image of a tree in a pinhole camera is:
qa.e: Rays from the top of the tree go down through the hole and rays from the bottom go up, so the image is inverted.

qa.q: When are our shadows the longest on a sunny day?
qa.e: When the Sun is low in the sky, shadows stretch out long.

qa.q: Which three things are needed to see a shadow?
qa.a: A light source, an opaque object and a screen
qa.e: Light must be blocked by an opaque object and fall on a surface for the shadow to be seen.

qa.q: Why can't you see a friend hiding around the corner of a wall?
qa.a: Light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around the wall
qa.e: Light from your friend would have to bend around the corner to reach your eyes, but it travels straight.

qa.q: What is reflection of light?
qa.a: The bouncing back of light from a surface
qa.e: When light hits a surface and bounces back, it is reflected.

qa.q: The angle of incidence is 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
qa.e: By the first law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

qa.q: A ray of light strikes a mirror making 50° with the mirror's surface. What is the angle of incidence?
qa.e: Angles are measured from the normal. 90° − 50° = 40°.

qa.q: The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is 80°. What is the angle of incidence?
qa.e: The normal splits the 80° equally, because both angles are equal: 80° ÷ 2 = 40°.

qa.q: What is the normal in reflection?
qa.a: A line at 90° to the mirror at the point where light hits
qa.e: The normal is drawn perpendicular to the mirror. Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from it.

qa.q: A ray of light falls on a mirror along the normal. In which direction does it reflect?
qa.a: Straight back along the same path
qa.e: The angle of incidence is 0°, so the angle of reflection is also 0°: the ray goes straight back.

qa.q: Which surface reflects light best to form clear images?
qa.e: Smooth, shiny surfaces reflect light regularly, so clear images form.

qa.q: Why is it dangerous to reflect sunlight into someone's eyes with a mirror?
qa.a: Strong reflected sunlight can damage the eyes
qa.e: Sunlight is very bright. Reflecting it into eyes can harm them, so never do it.

qa.q: Which of these describes the image in a plane mirror?
qa.e: A plane mirror gives an erect image of the same size as the object.

qa.q: Rohan stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is his image from him?
qa.e: The image is 2 m behind the mirror, so it is 2 + 2 = 4 m from Rohan.

qa.q: Why is 'AMBULANCE' written in mirror letters on the front of the vehicle?
qa.a: So drivers ahead can read it correctly in their mirrors
qa.e: A plane mirror swaps left and right, so the reversed word appears correct in the rear-view mirror.

qa.q: Swapping of left and right in a mirror image is called:
qa.e: Lateral means sideways. The image is inverted from side to side.

qa.q: Which mirror is used as the side mirror of vehicles because it shows a wider area?
qa.e: Convex mirrors give a wider view of the traffic behind.

qa.q: Dentists use which mirror to see an enlarged image of teeth?
qa.e: A concave mirror held close to the teeth gives an enlarged, upright image.

qa.q: The inner (hollow) side of a shiny steel spoon behaves like a:
qa.e: The inner side curves inwards like a cave, which makes it concave.

qa.q: A periscope helps you see over a wall. What does it use?
qa.e: Two plane mirrors, fixed at 45°, reflect light down the tube to your eye.

qa.q: What is the rotation of the Earth?
qa.e: Rotation is the Earth turning on its axis. Moving around the Sun is revolution.

qa.q: About how many hours does the Earth take to rotate once?
qa.e: One rotation takes about 24 hours, which gives us one day and one night.

qa.q: What is caused by the rotation of the Earth?
qa.e: As the Earth spins, the side facing the Sun has day and the other side has night.

qa.q: How many days are there in a leap year?
qa.e: A leap year has an extra day, 29 February, so it has 366 days.

qa.q: 2024 was a leap year. Which of these will be the next leap year?
qa.e: Leap years usually come every 4 years: 2024 + 4 = 2028.

qa.q: In which direction does the Earth rotate?
qa.e: The Earth turns from west to east. That is why the Sun, Moon and stars seem to move from east to west across the sky.

qa.q: What is one revolution of the Earth around the Sun?
qa.e: The Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to go once around the Sun.

qa.q: Which ancient Indian astronomer wrote that the Earth rotates on its axis?
qa.e: Aryabhata, about 1,500 years ago, explained the daily motion of the sky by the Earth's rotation.

qa.q: Why does the Moon shine?
qa.e: The Moon is like a giant mirror-ball lit by the Sun; it has no light of its own.

qa.q: On which night is the Moon not visible?
qa.e: On new moon, the Moon's lit side faces away from us.

qa.q: When the Moon's visible part grows each night, the Moon is said to be:
qa.e: Waxing means growing. It happens from new moon to full moon (Shukla Paksha).

qa.q: About how many days does the Moon take to go through all its phases once?
qa.e: One cycle of phases, from one new moon to the next, takes about 29 and a half days, roughly a month.

qa.q: Why do we see phases of the Moon?
qa.a: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it goes around the Earth
qa.e: The Moon is always round and half lit. Its position around the Earth changes how much of the lit half faces us.

qa.q: The period of the waning Moon, from full moon to new moon, is called:
qa.e: Shukla Paksha is the bright (waxing) half; Krishna Paksha is the dark (waning) half.

qa.q: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon from the Earth?
qa.a: The Moon spins once in the same time it takes to go around the Earth
qa.e: Because both take the same time, the same side keeps facing the Earth.

qa.q: A few days after the full moon, how will the Moon look?
qa.e: After full moon, the bright part shrinks night by night, so the Moon starts to wane.

qa.q: During a solar eclipse, which body is in the middle?
qa.e: The Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth and blocks the Sun's light.

qa.q: During a lunar eclipse, whose shadow falls on the Moon?
qa.e: The Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, so the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

qa.q: On which day can a lunar eclipse happen?
qa.e: Only at full moon is the Earth between the Sun and the Moon.

qa.q: Why don't we have a solar eclipse every new moon?
qa.a: The Moon's path is slightly tilted, so they usually do not line up exactly
qa.e: Most months the Moon passes a little above or below the line joining the Sun and the Earth.

qa.q: What is the safe way to watch a solar eclipse?
qa.e: Ordinary sunglasses are not safe. Only proper solar filters protect the eyes.

qa.q: Is it safe to watch a lunar eclipse with bare eyes?
qa.e: The Moon's light is just reflected sunlight and is gentle on the eyes, so a lunar eclipse can be watched safely.

qa.q: During a total lunar eclipse, how does the Moon often look?
qa.e: A little sunlight bends through the Earth's air and reaches the Moon, giving it a reddish glow.

qa.q: In a solar eclipse, whose shadow falls on the Earth?
qa.e: The Moon blocks sunlight, and its shadow falls on a part of the Earth.
